The Quiet Return of the Night Train

Ten years ago most European night trains had been cancelled, and travellers who wanted to cross the continent overnight had little choice but to fly. Today sleeper services are running again on many routes, and new carriages with private cabins are being delivered every month.

Why operators changed their minds

Operators say the change came from passengers who wanted to travel with a smaller carbon footprint and who were tired of airport security lines. A ticket for a couchette often costs less than a hotel room, and the traveller wakes up in the centre of the destination city.

Rail companies also found that night services make good use of track capacity that would otherwise sit empty, because freight and maintenance trains can share the same lines at different hours of the night.
